title: 8 Facilitation Rules Worth Unlearning (Especially If You're Good At This)
author: Nick Martin
summary: Nick Martin of WorkshopBank takes eight rules that beginning facilitators are commonly taught and argues that each has become a liability for experienced practitioners. He works through icebreakers unconnected to the work, the fear of silence, packed agendas, strict neutrality, slide decks, the feedback sandwich, full-day sessions and closing share rounds, offering a replacement practice for each. The recurring diagnosis is that most of these habits are the facilitator filling space or hiding behind a role when the group would do better work if the facilitator stepped back. His most developed argument concerns neutrality: he contends a facilitator should hold a view, reveal it only when it helps, and hand the decision back to the group, while staying out of genuine value calls. He also presses the economic case against bloated full-day sessions and recommends written commitments with owners and check-in dates in place of reflective go-rounds. The piece ends by reframing the facilitator's core question from which activities to use to what the group needs to achieve.
points: Martin recommends counting to at least ten after a question, because seconds six to ten are where people surface the less obvious and often best thought.
He argues that neutrality is the rule audiences see through fastest and that a facilitator should have an answer to every question asked.
The feedback sandwich is replaced with a plain three-part move: name the behaviour, name the impact, and ask a question.
He estimates a bloated full day yields about three hours of real work and urges designing for the least time the outcome needs.
Closing share rounds are dismissed as ritual in favour of written commitments with an owner and a check-in date within a fortnight.
quotes: Most of them come down to the same habit: the facilitator filling the space, or hiding inside a role, when the room would do better work if you got out of the way.
Silence after a question is thinking time. When you fill it, you do it because you're uncomfortable. And you take processing time away from the people who need it most.
Seconds six to ten are where someone lands the thought they weren't sure about. That thought is usually the best one in the room.
Neutrality is the rule most facilitators were trained hardest on, and the one the room sees through fastest.
Direct and kind beats it every time, and it's simpler: name the behaviour, name the impact, ask a question.
A bloated full day gives you about three hours of real work and five hours of diminishing returns, with people in the room and their heads somewhere else for the rest.
Going round the room to say how it went is a ritual, and rituals don't change what people do on Monday.
